title_html:
What if Mt. Fuji
were twice as tall?
title_plain: What if Mt. Fuji were twice as tall?
setting: August, at the lake below Mt. Fuji.

captions.html:
Mt. Fuji: 3,776 m.
August at the top: 6.4°C on average.

Let's double its height
and see what changes.

Then what if it were
3 times as tall?

effects.head:
Summer at the top:
about −18°C
effects.sub:
Air cools about 0.65°C every 100 m you climb.
Its August would feel like Fuji's January today (−18.2°C).

effects.head:
The snow
stops melting
effects.sub:
Even the warmest month stays far below 0°C,
so the white cap could last all year (estimate).

effects.head:
Each breath:
about 38% of the oxygen
effects.sub:
Air pressure at 7,500 m is about 383 hPa,
vs 1,013 hPa at sea level.

effects.head:
August at the top:
about −43°C
effects.sub:
Colder than Fuji's all-time record low
(−38.0°C, Feb 1981) — in midsummer.

effects.head:
The peak pokes into
the jet stream
effects.sub:
A river of wind at 30,000–40,000 ft.
It's why winter flights Fukuoka→Tokyo are
about 30 min faster than the other way.

end.html:
What we learned:
Height is climate.
1 km higher ≈ 6.5°C colder.

That's why Fuji keeps snow
while the town below is warm.

Assumptions

· Simple estimate: 0.65°C cooler per 100 m
· Real geology and weather are ignored

Sources

· Height: Geospatial Information Authority of Japan
· Summit normals 1991–2020, jet stream: JMA
· Record low −38.0°C: Ministry of the Environment
· Cooling rate: Heibonsha World Encyclopedia
· Pressure by altitude: standard altitude table

This is an AI simulation. It is not a real event.

caption:
What if Mt. Fuji were twice as tall? 🗻

At the summit (3,776 m), August averages 6.4°C (JMA normals, 1991–2020). Air cools about 0.65°C for every 100 m you climb — so a Fuji twice as tall would be roughly 24.5°C colder at the top.

① Summer at the top: about −18°C — like Fuji's January today (−18.2°C).
② Every month stays below freezing, so the snow cap could last all year (estimate).
③ At 7,500 m the air pressure is about 383 hPa vs 1,013 hPa at sea level: each breath holds about 38% of the oxygen.

At 3× (11,328 m):
④ August at the top: about −43°C — colder than Fuji's all-time record low of −38.0°C.
⑤ The peak reaches the jet stream (30,000–40,000 ft), the wind that makes winter flights Fukuoka→Tokyo about 30 min faster than Tokyo→Fukuoka.

What we learned: height is climate.

Sources: Geospatial Information Authority of Japan; Japan Meteorological Agency (summit normals; Haneda Airport Office jet stream notes); Ministry of the Environment; Heibonsha World Encyclopedia (lapse rate); standard altitude–pressure table.
Assumptions: simple estimate with a standard lapse rate; real geology and weather are ignored.

※ This is an AI simulation. It is not a real event.
